x: The backbone of the forest garden. The apple tree gives fruit, structure, shade, blossom and organic matter. We choose varieties suited to the Swedish climate and spread the harvest from early summer apples to winter apples that keep until Christmas. Apple trees need a pollination partner – another variety flowering at the same time – so planning matters. Keep the area around the trunk clear for the first years, so grass and herbs do not compete for water and nutrients.

l: Old Swedish varieties for juice, cake and winter stores
x: Sweden has hundreds of apple varieties, many bred or found on farms in the Mälaren valley. Some ripen in August and are to be eaten at once. Others are picked in October and improve after a few weeks in a cool cellar. Most are hard to find in an ordinary shop, but live on in old gardens and with fruit growers who have chosen flavour over durability in transport. On juicing day they are mixed – and the juice is better for it.

alt.x: Sweden has hundreds of apple varieties, many of them old farm varieties surviving in only a handful of trees. The national programme for cultivated diversity has surveyed and preserved many of them in gene banks and clone archives. Every apple pip gives a new, unique tree – which is why varieties are propagated by grafting, where a scion from an old tree is joined to a rootstock. An apple tree from a pip is seldom like its mother, but sometimes it becomes a new variety.

t: Common frog and smooth newt (Rana temporaria, Lissotriton vulgaris)
l: Rana temporaria, Lissotriton vulgaris – the pond’s spring folk
x: The common frog is often the first to spawn in the pond, sometimes only a few days after the ice has gone. The males purr low in the shallow water, and the females lay their spawn in large clumps that float up into the sun. After a couple of weeks the tadpoles hatch, and early in the summer tiny frogs creep up onto land. The smooth newt comes to the pond at the same time. During breeding the male grows a wavy crest along his back and an orange, spotted belly, and the female folds each egg separately into a leaf. The larvae breathe with feathery gills. Both species are protected, like all amphibians in Sweden. We look, but we do not take.

Three of the classic dye plants. Woad (Isatis tinctoria) gives blue, weld (Reseda luteola) gives clear yellow and the root of madder (Rubia tinctorum) gives red. All three can be grown in Sweden, and they give colour both to the weaving room’s yarn and to the studio’s watercolours. They are also beautiful in the garden – and weld is a plant much valued by pollinators.

t: Lingonberry and bilberry (Vaccinium vitis-idaea, Vaccinium myrtillus)
l: Vaccinium vitis-idaea and V. myrtillus – two dwarf shrubs in the same forest
x: Lingonberries and bilberries often grow side by side, but they differ in nature. The bilberry bush drops its leaves in autumn and thrives in shady, damp spruce forest. The lingonberry is evergreen, with glossy, leathery leaves, and wants more light – on rocky outcrops, in pine forest and in clearings. Bilberries ripen from July, lingonberries at the end of August and in September. Both live in partnership with fungi in the soil that help them take up nutrients from poor ground. Lingonberries contain substances that make them keep for a long time, and so for generations they have been stirred with a little sugar and set in the cellar. Even the sprigs are useful: in November they are bound into Advent wreaths.

Northern bat, Daubenton’s bat, brown long-eared bat and soprano pipistrelle. All of Sweden’s bats are protected. They need hollow trees, crevices in old buildings or bat boxes to sleep in by day, and darkness to hunt in by night. That is why we have as little outdoor lighting as possible, and the lighting we do have is warm, low and directed downwards.

Rose chafer, dor beetle, violet ground beetle, cockchafer, longhorn beetle, click beetle and burying beetle. Dead wood is one of the most threatened habitats in Sweden – about a fifth of the forest’s species depend on it. A woodpile, a fallen log or a tall stump is therefore one of the best contributions a garden can make.

The birch was one of the first trees to move into the Nordic countries after the inland ice, and it has followed the people here ever since. The bark is waterproof and almost indestructible: it has become baskets, shoes, roof underlay, rattles and letters. The sap is tapped in March and April and drunk fresh. Birch firewood burns hot and bright. In many northern cultures the birch has been a sacred tree – a world pillar linking earth and sky. At Vreta it stands around the pond and shades the granite boulders.

Europe’s largest woodpecker, coal black with a red crown. The black woodpecker’s large oval nest holes in old pines and aspens become, after a few years, homes for goldeneyes, tawny owls, stock doves and bats. It is therefore a keystone species – without it many others would have no home.

l: Elk, roe deer and wild boar – Alces alces, Capreolus capreolus, Sus scrofa
x: A skull tells a great deal about a life. The elk’s long, heavy head has a strong nasal bridge and teeth built for grinding twigs and bark. The roe deer’s light skull carries, in the buck, small knobbly antlers that are shed every autumn and grow back over the winter. The wild boar’s skull is wedge-shaped, with a strong neck for rooting in the soil and tusks that grow throughout life. Together they show three ways of living in the same forest: grazing, watchfulness and digging.

l: Humulus lupulus, Malus domestica, Hordeum vulgare
x: The brewery’s three plants. Hops climb several metres every summer and give cones full of bitter and aromatic compounds. The apple gives sugar, acidity and aroma to juice and cider. Barley is malted – allowed to sprout and dried – and becomes the basis of beer. All three can be grown around Uppsala, and together they show how a drink can have its roots in a place.

Sweden has some forty bumblebee species, and several of them are declining sharply. Bumblebees are particularly important pollinators in our climate because they can fly in cold and rain when honeybees stay at home. Different species have tongues of different lengths and prefer different flowers – so a diversity of flowers is needed to support a diversity of bumblebees. Red clover, bird’s-foot trefoil and knapweed are among their favourites.

Brimstone, orange-tip, red admiral, Camberwell beauty, small copper and silver-studded blue. Butterflies need two things: nectar for the adults and the right host plant for the caterpillars. The second part is often forgotten. A garden full of flowers but without nettles, bird’s-foot trefoil, alder buckthorn and cuckooflower may have butterfly visits – but no butterfly children.

The most underrated plant in Swedish nature. Young nettle leaves are nutritious and good – in soup, pie or as spinach. Nettles are the host plant for the caterpillars of the small tortoiseshell and the peacock. And they give biomass for the compost and nutrient-rich nettle feed as fertiliser. Use gloves, choose clean places to harvest, and limit their spread by keeping them in a bounded wild zone.

alt.x: The small tortoiseshell lays its eggs on the leaves of the stinging nettle. The caterpillars live together in a web and feed on the nettles until they pupate. Inside the pupa the caterpillar’s body dissolves almost entirely and is rebuilt into something quite different. After a few weeks a butterfly crawls out, unfolds its wings and flies. It is perhaps the clearest picture of transformation nature has to give – and it begins in the weed most people pull up.

x: Almost all the cabbage we eat is the same species, bred in different directions: the leaves in kale, the bud in white cabbage, the flower head in broccoli, the stem in kohlrabi. The swede is a species of its own, and has long been one of the most important winter vegetables in the Nordic countries. Kale can stand outside well into winter and be harvested leaf by leaf – it is the garden’s last green before the snow.

l: Theobroma cacao, Protium copal and Zea mays
x: For the Maya peoples cacao was a sacred drink taken at ceremonies, weddings and negotiations, and the beans were used as currency. Copal is the resin of tropical trees that is still burned as incense at Maya ceremonies today – it smells bright, citrusy and resinous. Maize is the grain of life. According to the *Popol Vuh*, the sacred book of the K’iche’ Maya, people were finally formed from maize dough, after several failed attempts with clay and wood.

Citrus trees originally come from south-east Asia and have been grown in the Mediterranean for more than a thousand years. The leaves are evergreen and fragrant when rubbed, and the flowers are among the most fragrant there are. Citrus wants slightly acid, rich and well-drained soil, regular feeding in summer and sparing watering in winter. The commonest reason a citrus tree drops its leaves is too much water in too dark a spot.

t: Red clover and white clover (Trifolium pratense, Trifolium repens)
x: Red clover is a short-lived nitrogen fixer suited to green manure and flowering areas. It is particularly valuable for bumblebees, whose long tongues reach the nectar in the deep flowers. White clover is low and creeping, tolerates trampling and suits paths and gaps where it protects the soil and fixes nitrogen. Both can be cut and used as mulch.

The soil builder above all others. Comfrey’s roots reach deep and bring up minerals other plants cannot reach. The large leaves can be cut three or four times a season and laid straight down as mulch under the fruit trees, where they break down quickly and become humus. Bumblebees love the flowers. Comfrey is not a food plant – it contains substances that can harm the liver – but it is one of the forest garden’s most important workers. Choose a sterile variety such as ‘Bocking 14’, and it will not spread by seed.

l: Corvus corax, Corvus cornix, Pica pica
x: Crows can recognise individual human faces, use tools and plan for the future. Whoever watches a magpie in the garden for a while sees an animal that is thinking all the time.

Wart-biter, great green bush-cricket, dark bush-cricket, meadow grasshopper and club-horned grasshopper. The Orthoptera are one of the clearest differences between a lawn and a meadow. They need grass that is allowed to grow tall and set seed – and in turn they are food for birds, frogs, grass snakes and bats.

The fjällko is one of Sweden’s native breeds – a small, hardy, hornless cow, usually white with black or red patches. It developed over centuries in the mountain and forest districts and is known for its protein-rich milk, which suits cheesemaking well. Today it is preserved as one of Sweden’s native breeds through active breeding work. Working with milk from native breeds is a way of keeping both knowledge and genetic heritage alive.

l: Blackbird, robin, chaffinch and willow warbler
x: The blackbird often sings before dawn, with a calm, melodious song. The robin starts early and also sings at dusk. The chaffinch’s trills end with a characteristic flourish. The willow warbler arrives in April and sings a falling, wistful phrase that for many is the very sound of the Swedish early summer.

Mistletoe (Viscum album) is Sweden’s only tree-dwelling parasite, but only half a parasite. It has its own green leaves and does its own photosynthesis, while water and nutrients are taken through a sucker that grows into the host tree’s vessels. In Sweden it is found mainly in the Mälaren valley and eastern Småland, most often on lime and maple but also on apple, hawthorn and poplar. It forks repeatedly and can grow nearly a metre across. The flowers come in April–May, and the white berries form only on female plants. The sticky flesh draws out into threads that stick to twigs when birds have eaten the berries – there the next mistletoe sprouts. In Norse myth it was a sprig of mistletoe that killed Baldr. Mistletoe is protected.

l: Aeshna cyanea, Libellula quadrimaculata, Sympetrum sanguineum
x: Southern hawker, four-spotted chaser and ruddy darter. All three live their first years as larvae on the bottom of the pond, where they eat mosquito larvae and small water creatures. A dragonfly larva can live for two or three years under water before it climbs up a stem, splits out of its skin and flies away. Leave the reeds standing over winter – that is where next year’s dragonflies emerge.

Dragonflies are the jewels of the pond. They live most of their lives as larvae under water – sometimes for several years – and then climb up a reed stem, split their skin and fly off as adults. As larvae they eat mosquito larvae and small water creatures; as adults they catch mosquitoes and flies in the air. A pond with dragonflies is a garden with fewer mosquitoes.

l: Corylus avellana – the first to flower
x: The hazel (Corylus avellana) flowers earlier than almost any other tree, often while the snow is still lying. The male flowers sit in the yellow catkins, which have hung on the branches since autumn and release their pollen on the wind as soon as a few days are mild. The female flowers are so small that most people never see them: a few red stigmas poking out of a bud. From them come nuts at the end of August and in September. The hazel thrives in the broadleaf woods and wooded pastures of the Mälaren valley, and its pollen is an early gift to the bees on a sunny day. By the entrance stands the corkscrew hazel, the threshold tree, with its twisted branches – the same species, the same catkins, only another form.

l: Polypody, male fern and ostrich fern
x: Ferns are among the oldest plants on earth – they existed long before the first flowers. They reproduce by spores rather than seeds, and in folk belief it was said that whoever found the fern’s flower on Midsummer night would gain the power to become invisible. There is no flower, but the myth says something about how mysterious they have been to people. Polypody grows on mossy stones and has a sweet root reminiscent of liquorice. Male fern thrives in shady forest, and ostrich fern unrolls its shoots like bishops’ crooks in spring. All three can grow on the living walls of the hall.

l: Pyrrhula pyrrhula, Fringilla coelebs, Loxia curvirostra
x: Rowan, hawthorn, rose hips and uncut seed heads in the meadow give the finches food through the winter. Whoever cuts everything down in autumn takes away their larder.

l: Linum usitatissimum – from blue flower to bed sheet
x: Flax has been grown in Sweden for thousands of years. The blue flower opens in the morning and drops its petals in the afternoon. From the stem’s fibres linen thread is spun and woven into linen – strong, cool and hard-wearing. From the seeds linseed oil is pressed, used to oil wood in the joinery. Wool from the sheep completes the picture: warm, moisture-regulating and self-cleaning. Together, flax and wool are the materials that make a Swedish bed a good bed.

l: Spring, file, rail and brake drum
x: Old steel is often better than new. The spring leaf becomes a chisel, the worn-out file a knife, the piece of rail an anvil and the brake drum a forge. The smith reads the scrap heap as a store – and always tests a small piece first.

t: Common frog and smooth newt (Rana temporaria, Lissotriton vulgaris)
x: Frogs and newts are the pond’s first sign of life – and some of the garden’s best slug hunters. The frog spawns early in spring in shallow, sun-warmed water and then lives most of the year on land. The newt seeks out the water in spring and overwinters under stones and in woodpiles. Both need a pond without fish, since fish eat spawn and larvae.

l: Apple, pear, plum, currant and sea buckthorn
x: The forest garden’s fruit and berries give both fresh food and stores. Apples for juice, purée and cakes. Pears and plums for compotes. Blackcurrants for cordial and jam. Sea buckthorn for marmalade and drinks – full of vitamin C. What is not eaten fresh is preserved, and what cannot be preserved goes to the hens or the compost.

l: Rye, spelt, barley and oats – and caraway
x: Rye has been grown in the Mälaren valley for more than a thousand years and copes with cold winters and poor soil. It gives a dark, tangy bread that keeps well. Spelt is an older wheat with a nutty flavour. Barley is one of the oldest cultivated grains in the Nordic countries and gives porridge, bread and malt. Oats thrive in the damp Swedish climate and give softness to bread and cakes. Caraway, which grows wild in the meadows of Uppland, gives rye bread its classic flavour. The café’s flour comes first and foremost from mills within 150 kilometres.

A pair with a striped chick on its back. The great crested grebe was close to extinction in the nineteenth century, when its feathers were used for ladies’ hats. Today it is one of the commonest and most visible birds in the bays of Ekoln.
n: Seen at Ekoln and the fens.

x: The leafy vegetables are the stars of the raised bed: fast, hardy and possible to harvest again and again. Lettuce and spinach bolt easily when the days are longest, so they are best sown early in spring and late in summer. Chard stands all season and tolerates both drought and frost, and its red and yellow stems make the bed beautiful. Rocket and Asian greens grow so fast that they can be sown several times in a season.

t: Green woodpecker and lesser spotted woodpecker
x: The green woodpecker depends on ants and on short-grazed or sparsely covered ground to search for them in. The lesser spotted woodpecker needs broadleaf woodland with plenty of dead and dying wood. Both are signs of a place that is allowed to age.

Harvestman and cellar spider. The harvestman has its body in a single piece and eats small creatures, dead insects and fungi – it is as much a cleaner as a hunter. The cellar spider has made itself at home in houses and likes to hunt other spiders, even house spiders many times its size.

Elephant hawk-moth, poplar hawk-moth, privet hawk-moth and pine hawk-moth. Hawk-moths can fly at more than fifty kilometres an hour and hover on the spot while they drink. The caterpillars are large and have a small horn at the rear. Whoever finds a hawk-moth caterpillar wandering across the path in late summer has seen a caterpillar on its way to bury itself and pupate in the soil – let it go.

The corkscrew hazel is a form of common hazel with twisted, corkscrew-like branches and curly leaves. It was discovered in an English hedge in the nineteenth century and has since been propagated as an ornamental tree. Early in spring, before the leaves open, the yellow catkins hang from the branches and give pollen to the first bumblebees. Hazelnuts form sparingly. In winter the bare crown becomes a sculpture – and that is when it looks its very best as a threshold tree by a gate.

The hedgehog (Erinaceus europaeus) is the garden’s night watchman. In one night it can wander several kilometres and eat slugs, beetles and caterpillars. It needs holes in fences to move between gardens, brush and leaf piles to overwinter in, and gardens without poison. Since 2024 the European hedgehog has been classed as near threatened on the international Red List – every garden that welcomes it makes a difference.

Swedish native breeds have developed over hundreds of years together with Swedish farms and the Swedish climate. They lay fewer eggs than modern hybrids but are hardier, more independent and better at foraging. They are living heritage – and some of the place’s busiest workers.

l: Dill, chives, lovage, thyme, sage and parsley
x: The culinary herbs grow at the bed edges near the kitchens – permaculture’s zone 1, where what you need every day should be close. Dill and chives for the herring and the potatoes, lovage that gives soups a stock flavour, thyme and sage for what is fried and grilled. Many are perennial and come back year after year, and when they flower they are full of bees.

l: Lime, goat willow, white clover, rosebay willowherb and heather
x: Goat willow is the most important flower of spring for bees and bumblebees – its catkins flower as early as April, when almost nothing else does. White clover gives nectar all summer. The limes flower in July and can give large quantities of pale, fragrant honey. Rosebay willowherb takes over clearings and roadsides in August, and heather ends the season with a dark, strong honey. The plate also shows the honeybee and the buff-tailed bumblebee.

Worker and queen at the nest. The hornet also hunts at dusk and is sometimes drawn to lit windows in late summer. A colony lives only one season: in autumn all die except the young queens, which overwinter in rotting wood and start new nests the next spring. An old nest is never used again.

Marmalade hoverfly, drone fly and banded hoverflies, a cuckoo wasp and a parasitic wasp on an umbellifer. Umbelliferous plants – cow parsley, dill, carrot and wild parsnip – are the favourites of hoverflies and small wasps, since the nectar sits shallow and is easy to reach for short mouthparts.

The waxwing breeds in the coniferous forests of northern Sweden and Russia and comes south in winter, when the rowan berries run out further north. Some years it comes in large flocks, other years hardly at all. It is recognised by its crest, black eye mask and the small red wax-like tips on its wing feathers, which have given it its English name. The Swedish name, sidensvans, refers to its silky plumage. A waxwing can eat several hundred rowan berries a day. It swallows them whole, and the seeds are spread in its droppings – so the birds plant new rowans. A rowan in the forest garden is therefore an investment in both winter birds and new trees.

l: Vulpes vulpes – the one who walks in its own tracks
x: The fox wears its thickest coat in January, and the bushy tail becomes a blanket when it sleeps curled up in the snow. It hunts voles it hears under the snow cover: stands still, tilts its head, leaps high and comes down front paws first. This is called mousing. January and February are the mating season, and the cubs are born in April–May in an earth, often one that a badger once dug. The track is easy to recognise. The paws are set almost in a straight line, and the hind foot treads in the forefoot’s print. The fox eats whatever there is – vole, hare, bird, berries, insects and carrion. It is the place’s most faithful winter guest and writes its line in the snow every night.

l: Aeshna cyanea – guardian of the pond
x: The southern hawker is one of the large dragonflies that patrol the pond from July until well into autumn. The male is dark with green and blue spots, the female greener and browner. It is curious and likes to fly up to take a closer look at whoever is sitting by the water. But most of its life is spent beneath the surface. The larva lives in the pond for a couple of years and hunts insect larvae and tadpoles with a folding lower lip that shoots out at lightning speed. One summer night it climbs up a reed stem, its skin splits along the back and the dragonfly crawls out. The larval skin stays on the stem.

Red clover is one of the meadow’s most important plants, both for the soil and for the insects. In small nodules on the roots live bacteria that take nitrogen from the air and make it available to the plant. That is why it manages on poor soil where many other plants starve. The nectar sits deep in the flowers’ narrow tubes, and it is mainly bumblebees that reach it. The red-tailed bumblebee, black with a red tail, is one of the visitors. When red clover began to be grown in New Zealand in the nineteenth century it set almost no seed – not until bumblebees had been shipped there from England. No bumblebees, no clover.

The kingfisher digs its nest in a vertical earth bank near water and fishes from a low branch or a reed stem. It is vulnerable to hard winters when the water freezes, and numbers vary greatly between years.
n: Seen at Ekoln and the fens.

x: Four of the oldest machines there are. The lever trades force for distance, the wedge holds what is lifted, the rollers turn friction into movement and the block and tackle lets one person lift what would otherwise take four. None of them needs fuel – only sense, patience and respect for the weight.

Lizards need sun, warmth and hiding places. A south-facing stone wall or stone pile, with gaps to crawl into and a little bare sand nearby for egg-laying, may be enough for them to move in. The sand lizard is protected in Sweden and suffers from overgrowth and tidy gardens. It eats insects, spiders and small slugs.

l: Tussilago farfara, Hepatica nobilis, Anemone nemorosa – the three steps of spring
x: Three flowers mark the start of spring at Vreta, roughly in this order. Coltsfoot comes first, on bare soil in sunny spots, with yellow flowers that open before the leaves have shown. The leaves, shaped like a horse’s hoof, come once flowering is over. The name *Tussilago* comes from the Latin word for cough. Hepatica flowers on the slopes of the broadleaf woods, and its seeds are spread by ants drawn to a small nutritious appendage. The wood anemone comes last and spreads in carpets through its rhizomes. All three use the same gap in the year: the light that reaches the ground before the canopy closes.

l: Cuculus canorus – the messenger of spring
x: The cuckoo (Cuculus canorus) winters in tropical Africa and arrives in Uppland at the beginning of May. The female builds no nest of her own. Instead she lays one egg at a time in the nests of other small birds – meadow pipit, reed warbler and white wagtail are among the commonest hosts. Each female usually keeps to one host species, and her eggs resemble the host’s. The young cuckoo hatches first and pushes out the other eggs, and is then raised by foster parents much smaller than itself. The adult cuckoos leave Sweden as early as July and August. The young migrate later, alone, and still find their way to Africa.

l: Hose, measuring rod, plumb line and branding iron
x: Building’s oldest measuring tools are still some of the most reliable. The water level carries a height round corners, the plumb line shows the vertical, the story pole carries every measurement to be repeated and the branding iron marks the timber so the mark remains for generations.

l: Oxeye daisy, harebell, red clover and more
x: Seven kinds of flowers under the pillow is one of the oldest Swedish Midsummer traditions. The meadow at Vreta gives them all: ox-eye daisy, harebell, red clover, buttercup, wood cranesbill, yarrow and lady’s bedstraw. Picking them is also a way of getting to know the meadow – and seeing how rich in species it has become.

l: Mugwort, yarrow, St John’s wort and valerian
x: Many plants have been associated with the moon and the night. Mugwort, a close relative of wormwood, has a long history in folk medicine and ritual and was said to protect the traveller from weariness – it was put in the shoes before long journeys. Yarrow was a healing plant for wounds and was used in China as the stalks cast for the *I Ching*. St John’s wort flowers around Midsummer, when the light is strongest. Valerian has a sweet, strong scent that cats love. Several of them can be poisonous or interact with medicines, and at Vreta they are used in incense, in wreaths and in the garden – not as medicine.

l: Lime hawk-moth, elephant hawk-moth and garden tiger
x: Moths are as important pollinators as bees, but they work while we sleep. They seek out flowers that are fragrant and glow at dusk: honeysuckle, dame’s violet and evening primrose. By planting night-flowering plants near the rooms and keeping the outdoor lighting low, we give them a place – and the guests a scent to fall asleep to.

l: Amanita muscaria – beautiful, mythical and poisonous
x: No mushroom has had to carry as many myths as the fly agaric (Amanita muscaria). It has been linked with shamans in Siberia, with the Vikings’ berserkers, with gnomes and elves and with the red and white colours of Christmas. But it is poisonous and can cause severe poisoning, and it must never be eaten. At Vreta it glows in the meadow grass in autumn, and we leave it standing. It reminds us that the sacred and the dangerous often grow in the same place – and that reverence sometimes means leaving well alone.

The stinging nettle is one of Vreta’s fifteen key plants and perhaps the most misunderstood. It stings, spreads and takes up room – and so it is weeded out of most gardens. But it is the host plant for the caterpillars of the small tortoiseshell, the peacock and the red admiral, it gives nourishing soup in May and fibre that has been woven into cloth for thousands of years. In folk belief the nettle protected against evil powers. At Vreta it is left standing at the edges, as a reminder that what is uncomfortable can also be sacred.

l: Tawny owl, hedgehog, bat and moths
x: The tawny owl likes to breed in old trees and nest boxes and is heard best in late autumn and late winter. The hedgehog is the garden’s night watchman and eats slugs, caterpillars and beetles – it needs leaf piles and brush piles to overwinter. The bats hunt insects over water and along woodland edges; a single soprano pipistrelle can eat thousands of midges in a night. All of them benefit from a place with darkness, water and variety.

Honeyberry, sea buckthorn and aronia have in common that they cope with cold winters, wind and poor soil better than most berries. Honeyberry flowers as early as April and tolerates frost during flowering. Sea buckthorn thrives in sun and well-drained soil and can send up suckers. Aronia is almost entirely free of disease. Together they lengthen the berry season from June to October.

l: Pyrrhula pyrrhula – the red lantern of winter
x: The bullfinch is winter’s clearest colour. The male has a rose-red breast and rose-red cheeks, the female is grey-brown, and both wear a glossy black cap. The Swedish name, domherre, is usually explained by the bird’s resemblance to a cathedral canon in his dark skullcap. Bullfinches often stay together in pairs even in winter and move calmly and almost silently through the thickets. They eat buds and seeds of ash, maple and weeds, and from rowan berries they take only the seeds – the flesh often ends up in the snow under the tree. In winter northern bullfinches come south and join those already here. A pair on a snowy spruce bough is November’s best colour picture.

l: Quercus robur – the tree that remembers
x: The oak can live for more than a thousand years, and few trees carry so much life: hundreds of species of insects, lichens, fungi and birds live on and in an old oak. It has been sacred in many cultures – to Thor in the north, to Zeus in Greece and to the druids in the Celtic lands. In the area around Vreta stands a very old oak with deeply furrowed bark and wide, twisting branches. It was here long before us, and with a little luck it will stand long after.

The jay (Garrulus glandarius) is a pinkish-brown member of the crow family, with a white rump and a brilliant blue wing patch with fine black bars. For most of the year it is shy, but in October it is seen everywhere. Then it gathers acorns, several at a time in its throat and beak, and hides them one by one in the ground, often far from the oak. A single jay can hide several thousand acorns in an autumn. It finds most of them again, even under snow, but not all. That is how oaks travel. Many young oaks at woodland edges and in pastures have been planted by jays, and the old oak at Vreta may very well be one of them.

The tawny owl (Strix aluco) is Sweden’s commonest owl and one of the place’s most important residents. It hunts voles and mice at night and keeps the rodents in balance – free of charge and without poison. A nest box of the right size, placed high in a quiet tree, can become a home for generations.

l: Rheum, Allium ursinum, Crambe maritima, Helianthus tuberosus
x: Rhubarb, ramsons, sea kale and Jerusalem artichoke. Perennial vegetables build root systems that go deep and come back year after year without the soil needing to be worked. They suit the forest garden’s herb layer perfectly. Rhubarb leaves contain oxalic acid and should not be eaten – but they make excellent mulch. Ramsons should only be picked where they grow in abundance, and never confused with the poisonous lily of the valley, which has similar leaves.

Common buzzard, osprey, sparrowhawk and white-tailed eagle. The birds of prey stand at the top of the food web and are a measure of the health of the whole system. Without voles and mice, no buzzards; without fish, no ospreys. That they are here means there is plenty of what they live on.
n: Seen over Ekoln, the fens and the fields.

x: Both breed in tree holes and nest boxes and live almost entirely on insects. In one breeding season a pair can feed their young thousands of caterpillars and flies – invaluable help in the forest garden.

l: Ribes nigrum, R. rubrum, R. uva-crispa
x: Currants and gooseberries have been grown in Swedish gardens for several hundred years – on a larger scale since the eighteenth century – and wild currants still grow along streams and woodland edges. Blackcurrants such as ‘Öjebyn’, from Norrbotten, are so hardy that they cope almost anywhere in the country. The leaves can be dried for tea, and the flowers in May are among the first the bumblebees visit. Let the birds have their share – or cover with netting when the berries ripen.

Juniper has been used for smoking and cleansing for thousands of years. Spruce resin smells of forest and warmth. Lavender calms, and wormwood, like its relative mugwort, has a long history in folk medicine and ritual. Together they become the basis of the incense for Vreta’s retreats. Wormwood is bitter and strong and is used only in small amounts.

The robin builds its nest low, ideally in a brush hedge, a woodpile or a dense thicket. It likes to follow whoever is digging in the garden, on the hunt for worms and grubs that come up into the light. It is one of the birds that stay longest into the autumn – and sometimes all winter – if there is shelter and food.

l: Elder, blackcurrant, rhubarb and sea buckthorn
x: The elder’s flower heads are picked in June in the morning when they smell strongest, and the berries in September – but only ripe and cooked, since raw berries and green parts can cause nausea. Blackcurrants are rich in vitamin C and give the darkest cordial. Rhubarb is really a vegetable but is used as fruit; the leaves are poisonous and go to the compost. Sea buckthorn’s orange berries are so sour and so rich in vitamin C that they are seldom eaten straight from the bush – but in marmalade and cordial they are unbeatable.

A Swedish coastal plant that has it all: silvery leaves, orange berries full of vitamin C, and the ability to fix nitrogen with the help of actinomycetes in its roots. Sea buckthorn thrives in sun and well-drained soil and tolerates both drought and wind. It is dioecious, so both male and female plants are needed to get berries. It can send up suckers, so give it a place where that does no harm.

l: Marigold, poppy, cornflower, sunflower, dill, beans and peas
x: Every seed is a whole plant at rest. The pot marigold’s curved, prickly seeds, the poppy’s capsule with hundreds of tiny black grains, the cornflower’s plumed seeds and the sunflower’s striped kernels look quite different – but all carry everything needed to begin again. Beans and peas are the easiest to save: leave a few pods on until they rustle, and pick out the seeds. Dill and many meadow flowers sow themselves if you let them.

t: Cep and chanterelle (Boletus edulis, Cantharellus cibarius)
l: Boletus edulis and Cantharellus cibarius – companions of the trees
x: Cep and chanterelle are often found in the same forest, and that is no accident. Both live in mycorrhiza, an exchange with the trees’ roots in which the fungus gives water and minerals and receives sugar back. That is why they do not grow just anywhere, but near spruce, pine and birch. The chanterelle is recognised by its egg-yolk colour, its faint scent of apricot and its low, branching ridges instead of gills. The cep has a thick stem with a fine white net at the top and pores instead of gills. The bitter bolete resembles it but is bitter, with pink pores and a dark net on the stem. Never eat a mushroom you are not completely sure of.

The grass snake is protected, like all Swedish reptiles. It needs sun-warmed stones, water with frogs and a warm, damp heap of compost or leaves to lay its eggs in. The young hatch in August–September, about fifteen centimetres long and already fully independent.

alt.l: Natrix natrix – guardian of the pond
alt.x: The grass snake is recognised by the yellow or white patches behind its head. It is completely harmless to people and would rather flee than defend itself – at worst it plays dead or gives off a foul-smelling liquid. It swims skilfully and hunts frogs, toads and fish. The females lay their eggs in the warmth of compost heaps and manure piles, and so the grass snake has long lived close to people. In old Swedish folk belief it was the farm’s protective animal, which was given milk in a bowl and must not be harmed. The grass snake is protected in Sweden.

x: The earthworm is the best known of the soil’s workers – Darwin wrote a whole book about it. But it has the company of thousands of others: springtails and mites that break organic matter into fine pieces, woodlice that break down leaves, beetle larvae, roundworms, and above all fungi whose threads can form networks kilometres long in a single cubic metre of soil. Together they are the soil’s digestive system.

l: Rhagonycha fulva, Coccinella septempunctata, Adalia bipunctata
x: Ladybirds overwinter in large clusters in bark crevices, under leaves and in window frames. Whoever clears away all the fallen leaves in autumn clears away next year’s aphid control.

l: Passer domesticus, Passer montanus, Prunella modularis
x: House sparrow, tree sparrow and dunnock. Sparrows need a dense hedge to hide in, seeds and spilt grain – and insects for their young. The hen run, with its spilt feed and its dust baths, is one of their favourite places.

Garden spider, four-spot orb-weaver, wasp spider, house spider and mouse spider. Sweden has about 700 spider species, and almost all are completely harmless to people. A garden spider can catch hundreds of insects in a season. Leave the webs in the meadow in autumn – they are both a larder and one of the loveliest sights of the year.

The stone fruits – plums and cherries – have a hard stone around the seed, while pears and apples have a core. Plums and cherries flower early and are important for the first bees in spring. The pear can grow very old – there are pear trees in Swedish gardens more than two hundred years old. All three belong to the rose family, related to both the raspberry and the strawberry.

l: Peppermint, lemon balm, camomile, raspberry leaf, rosehip and lime blossom
x: The tea in the café is blended from herbs from the garden. Peppermint and lemon balm grow almost too easily and need keeping in check. Camomile is sown every spring and gives small white flowers that are dried whole. Raspberry leaves are picked young and dried into a soft, mild tea. Rose hips from the dog rose and other wild roses are harvested after the first frost, and lime blossom is picked in July when it smells strongest. Dried and blended they become the café’s own teas – and are sold in bags in the shop.

Flax (Linum usitatissimum) is one of the oldest cultivated plants in the Nordic countries. From the stem comes fibre that becomes linen thread – strong, cool and hard-wearing – and from the seeds come linseed and linseed oil, which in turn becomes the binder in the artists’ studio’s paints. Flax flowers pale blue for a short time in summer. Following it from seed to thread is to understand how much work lies in a single piece of cloth.

The hazel is one of our oldest cultivated plants – people have eaten hazelnuts in Sweden since the Stone Age. In the forest garden it fills the shrub layer and the woodland edge, gives nuts in autumn and early pollen to the bees as early as March, when the catkins flower. It also gives nesting places and food to birds and small animals. Hazel tolerates pruning and can be coppiced to give straight rods for bean supports and wattle.
n: The plate shows the hazel with catkins, nuts and a squirrel by the stump.

x: Great tit, blue tit, coal tit, crested tit, marsh tit and long-tailed tit. A pair of great tits can feed their young 10,000 caterpillars in one brood. Nest boxes with the right hole size – 28 mm for blue tits, 32 mm for great tits – are among the simplest and most effective things we can do.

t: The animals of the four winds
l: Condor, jaguar, hummingbird and anaconda – Vultur gryphus, Panthera onca, Trochilidae and Eunectes murinus
x: The Andean condor has a wingspan of more than three metres and can glide for hours on the warm winds over the mountains without beating its wings. The jaguar is the largest cat of the Americas and likes to swim. Hummingbirds are the world’s smallest birds: the wings beat so fast that they hum, and they can hover and fly backwards. The green anaconda is the world’s heaviest snake and lives mostly in water. The flower on the plate is *Cantua buxifolia*, the sacred flower of the Inca, which is today Peru’s national flower and is pollinated by hummingbirds.

t: The four winds of the north
l: White-tailed eagle, brown bear, bee and grass snake – Haliaeetus albicilla, Ursus arctos, Apis mellifera and Natrix natrix
x: The same order, the same directions – different animals. The white-tailed eagle is the largest bird of prey in the Nordic countries, with a wingspan of up to two and a half metres. The brown bear is Sweden’s largest predator and sleeps through the winter in a den. The honeybee and the bumblebee pollinate the red clover, and heather gives the dark heather honey. The grass snake is recognised by the yellow patches behind its head. It is completely harmless and lays its eggs where it is warm – in the compost, in the manure heap or in a pile of rotting leaves – and where the old breaks down, the new hatches.

The white wagtail is one of our birds most closely tied to people. It likes to follow whoever is digging or mowing and picks up the insects that are disturbed. When it returns in April you know the ice will soon have gone from the bays of Ekoln.

l: Iris pseudacorus, Caltha palustris, Lythrum salicaria
x: Yellow flag, marsh marigold and purple loosestrife belong at the pond’s edge and on a wetland raft. Their roots take up nutrients from the water, give shelter to frogs and larvae and bind the shore. All three are native and flower in turn from spring to late summer.

Red mason bee, mining bee, leafcutter bee, buff-tailed bumblebee and red-tailed bumblebee. More than half of our wild bees live in the ground. So the simplest way to help them is not a bee hotel but a sunny patch of bare, undisturbed soil or sand – and flowers from early spring to late autumn.

Stinging nettle, ground elder, dandelion and fat hen. What grows of its own accord in a garden is often the most nutritious – and it needs no sowing, no watering and no feeding. Pick young leaves early in the season, when they are mildest, and choose places free of pollution and dog walking. Nettles must be cooked or dried before they are eaten, so that the stinging hairs disappear.

Two of the most useful shrubs on a place like Vreta. Hazel is coppiced and gives straight rods for bean poles, trellises and handles. Willow grows fast in damp soil, gives supple withies for wattle and takes root from a rod pushed into the ground – a living building material that renews itself every year.

alt.l: Salix – the tree of water and renewal
alt.x: The willow grows where it is damp and roots almost by itself: a twig pushed into wet soil often has roots after a few weeks. That is why it has become a symbol of renewal and vitality in many cultures. Young willow shoots contain substances that help other cuttings to root, and the bark contains salicin – the substance that once gave rise to acetylsalicylic acid. At Vreta willow is used for cuttings, woven fences, baskets and willow water – and thin, straight willow twigs can become the core of home-made incense.

l: Rowan, spruce, juniper, rosehip and mistletoe
x: Winter is not empty. The rowan berries glow when everything else is grey and feed waxwings and thrushes. Spruce and juniper give greenery, scent and material for wreaths. The rose hips stay on well into winter. Gathering Christmas decorations on the place – without taking more than the plants can bear – is part of the preparations for the Christmas market.

Every kind of wood has its qualities. Oak is heavy, hard and durable – the classic building timber for what must last for centuries. Birch is tough and fine to carve, and suits handicraft. Ash is elastic and strong, perfect for handles and bent parts. Pine is light, straight and resinous, and has been Sweden’s most important building timber. Whoever knows their woods knows which suits which task.
Woodlouse, centipede and millipede. None of them does much harm to living plants. They are the soil’s cleaning staff – and food for hedgehogs, shrews, frogs and birds.

Three simple constructions that transform a workshop. The French cleat lets the tools move without new holes. The cyclone catches the shavings before they reach the filter. The wheeled base with folding wheels lets a machine of several hundred kilos be rolled aside – and stand firm when it is used.

l: Piano, guitar, cello, frame drum, tall drum, didgeridoo, flute, willow whistle and rattle
x: An old encyclopaedia showed instruments as they are built: a resonating body, something that vibrates and something that sets it moving. The drum’s skin, the flute’s column of air and the strings of the cello, the guitar and the piano are different ways of making the air sing – in the piano small felt-covered hammers strike the strings when the keys are pressed. The willow whistle is made in spring, when the sap rises and the bark comes away from the wood: a cut, a few taps with the knife handle and the bark can be pulled off like a stocking. It lasts only a few days – but it is perhaps the most Swedish instrument of all.
